Q: Is it possible to know if a Device is in Airplane Mode or not via JavaScript? A:

Thinking out loud. Through an on-line translator, but I hope you will understand.

JS is a high-level language, so getting access to low-level system information on a device is a problem for it due to security concerns.

Considering that in the end you need to get data about the activation of the "flight mode", then, I suppose, we are talking about a mobile device. The easiest way is to simply track down publicly available data. For example, a network.

There are two options here:

1. Use navigator.onLine.

Returns true/false

help

true - does not guarantee Internet access, because the same response will come, for example, when connecting to a local network without Internet access, etc.

false - does not mean airplane mode, because the same response will come, for example, when WiFi is disabled or the mobile network is weak.

2. In my opinion, more interesting.

const net = await fetch('http://localhost:8080/health', {
      method: 'HEAD',
      cache: 'no-store'
});

Returns net.ok / error

Or just check for:

true - the server has responded.

false - the request failed. We are no longer interested in the reason (there is no network, the server is turned off, timeout, connection error, etc. It does not matter).

------

But personally, I would check the "flight mode" for secondary signs. The ability to activate bluetooth or WiFi using the same navigator.

This approach is guaranteed to work on Chrome (Android, Windows, macOS). I haven't checked the rest, so I can't confirm.

For example, bluetooth using the Web Bluetooth API

here you can read about it 

if ('bluetooth' in navigator) {
  navigator.permissions.query({ name: 'bluetooth' }).then(result => {
    console.log('Bluetooth permission state:', result.state);
  });
}

This request is highly likely to cause a pop-up window on the device to grant permission to access the device, if it is active, and show its status (granted, denied, prompt).

or it will throw an exception if there is no access.

Q: N*N sized Identity Matrix using Higher Order Functions A:

Every answer here makes me go "this is so weird".

Weirder still, I don't know any alternative that isn't also weird.

But here is an answer that isolates the weirdness into a separate function, which makes me feel a little better.

const make_array = (n,f) => Array.from({length:n}, (_,i) => f(i));  // weird
const identitymatrix = n => make_array(n, irow => 
                              make_array(n, icol =>
                                icol==irow ? 1 : 0));
console.log(identitymatrix(3));

Q: Can I re-use a PreparedStatement if it hits a transient exception? A:

Since the API does not provide much information about the behavior when SQLTransientException happens apart from below

when the driver has determined that the timeout value that was specified by the setQueryTimeout method has been exceeded and has at least attempted to cancel the currently running Statement

Verified the Mysql JDBC4 Implementation .

In my observation, I could see there is one possible SQLTimeoutException (i.e SQLTransientException ) can happen if the timed out.

And while timed out , it is not just clearing the last statements , it is clearing entire Batch ( at least in MYSQL Implementation )

// we timeout the entire batch, not individual statements

So that part is clear.

And as per JDBC Specification

The statement’s batch is reset to empty once executeBatch returns

Irrespective of executeBatch throws exception / succeed it would clear the Batch .

Specifically Mysql Prepared Statement clears the batch at finaly block in executeBatch() method

finally {
        this.statementExecuting.set(false);
        clearBatch();
        }

So your logic will not work, since you are not adding the statements into batch again.

So add the statements back to batch and re-execute . there are highly possible you might end up in Timeout again. So first find the time out . if possible write some information about cause / state in the execution logs.

Q: Ansible provisioning azure vm with random name A:

Indeed, the %01x format specifiers in name: "vm-{{env}}-sql-{{resource_odd_string}}-{{'%01x'|format(item)}}" turns decimal numbers to hexadecimal (101 → 0x65 but without the prefix).

Use the %03d format speficier if you want to always get a three digit decimal integer (65 → 065, 101 → 101).
